items.title: The Only Way to Debug AI Agents at Scale
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
Building an AI agent is straightforward.

But running hundreds of agents reliably in production is HARD.

An agent might work perfectly during development, yet fail at scale in production. It could get stuck in a reasoning loop, call the wrong tool, exceed its token budget, or return an incorrect answer.

And when something goes wrong, you need to identify which step caused the failure.

Traditional application monitoring works, but AI agents create new challenges. Their execution paths vary, they make decisions at runtime, and a single user request could trigger multiple agents, tool calls, and model invocations.

This is where an AI agent harness comes into play.

An agent harness provides the infrastructure & controls around a Large Language Model () to manage its execution.

A production-ready agent harness includes these components:

  • Plan tasks, execute actions, observe results, and adjust the execution plan when necessary.

  • Context and memory management: Manage the agent’s context window, preserve execution state, and retrieve relevant information from short-term or long-term memory.

  • Measure response quality, task completion, and agent behavior using ground-truth datasets, automated checks, or LLM-as-a-Judge.

  • Enforce authentication, authorization, and access controls across applications, agents, tools, and data sources.

  • Detect and mitigate risks such as prompt injection, unauthorized tool use, and memory poisoning.

  • Human-in-the-loop (HITL): Allow users/operators to review decisions, approve sensitive actions, and intervene during execution.

These components make agent execution more reliable.

Yet you still need visibility into how agents behave once they enter production. That’s where observability becomes critical. You need to trace every agent execution, identify failures, measure response quality, and understand each workflow's cost.

  • How reasoning, orchestration, memory, and tools work together in an agentic system.

  • End-to-end observability: How to trace agent executions across models, tools, and external services.

  • Which trace identifiers and attributes let you track agent behavior across distributed systems.

  • How to measure task success, response quality, and tool usage using telemetry and automated evaluations.

  • How to estimate infrastructure and inference costs, measure token usage, and optimize agent performance at scale.

Agentic AI Reference Architecture

For simple tasks, a single agent is enough…

But complex workflows require many specialized agents to work together.

Imagine an AI research assistant tasked with analyzing a company’s financial performance:

  • One agent retrieves financial reports,

  • Another agent analyzes the numbers,

  • And a third agent prepares the final summary.

An orchestration engine coordinates their execution & manage task dependencies.

Let’s examine the key components:

1. Reasoning and Orchestration

The reasoning layer determines how an agent approaches a task.

For a complex request, the planner breaks the original goal into smaller subtasks. The orchestration engine then coordinates their execution, handles dependencies, and collects the results.

Here are two popular approaches that let agents reason and execute tasks:

  • A prompting technique that encourages a model to work through intermediate reasoning steps before producing an answer. It supports complex problem-solving but does not provide task orchestration.

  • Reasoning and Acting (ReAct): An agent pattern that alternates between reasoning, tool execution, and observations. The agent uses tool results to decide its next action and adjust its plan.

A research agent might search for a company’s annual report, extract its revenue figures, and calculate year-over-year growth. If the report is unavailable, the agent could choose another source.

The orchestration engine manages this execution flow, with retries, task dependencies, and termination conditions.

2. Agent Discovery and Composition

When multiple agents collaborate, the system needs a way to discover their capabilities and determine which agent should handle each task.

An agent registry maintains descriptions of available agents, their supported operations, and their access requirements.

The Agent2Agent () protocol provides a standardized way for agents to communicate and discover capabilities through an Agent Card.

An Agent Card is a JSON document containing this data:

  • Agent’s name, description, and provider information.

  • The address where other apps/agents access its A2A service.

  • Supported features, such as streaming & push notifications.

  • Security requirements for accessing the agent.

  • Tasks the agent supports, including descriptions, identifiers, and input/output formats.

An orchestration system discovers a financial analysis agent through its Agent Card and delegates a relevant task to it.

A2A supports interoperability between agents built using different frameworks.

A centralized marketplace is optional; agents could also be discovered through configured endpoints or registries.

3. Agent Integration and Tool Access

Once agents are selected, they need a way to communicate with other agents, applications, and external services.

The integration layer supports several interaction patterns:

  • One agent delegates work to another through an API or an agent communication protocol.

  • An agent exchanges data with an application or returns results for users.

  • A user initiates a task or provides additional instructions.

  • An agent requests human approval/intervention before continuing a workflow.

The Model Context Protocol () provides a standardized interface for AI applications to interact with external systems.

MCP uses a client-server architecture and exposes three capabilities:

  • Data and contextual information exposed by an MCP server.

  • Functions an AI app could invoke to retrieve information or perform actions.

  • Reusable prompt templates exposed by an MCP server.

A research agent could use an MCP server to retrieve documents from an enterprise knowledge base. Another tool could query a database or create a report.

MCP standardizes interactions between AI apps and external capabilities, while A2A focuses on communication between agents.

Both protocols could coexist within the same architecture.

4. Context and Memory Management

Complex agents execute multiple steps over extended periods.

So they need to preserve relevant information between actions and across separate sessions.

Memory management lets agents maintain context without repeatedly processing the entire interaction history.

Here are three key components:

  • Information currently available within the model’s context window--instructions, recent messages, and tool results.

  • Persistent information about workflow progress, completed tasks, pending actions, and checkpoints.

  • Information retained across interactions, such as user preferences, past outcomes, or retrieved knowledge.

For semantic memory, one common approach is to convert text into numerical representations called embeddings and store them in a vector database.

The database retrieves semantically similar information using similarity measures such as cosine similarity or inner product.

At scale, Approximate Nearest Neighbor () search accelerates retrieval by trading some accuracy for faster searches. Maximum Inner Product Search () is one possible retrieval objective.

Yet vector databases are only one part of memory management.

Execution state belongs in a durable database or checkpoint store. Structured records and conversation histories use other storage systems.

The architecture should select the appropriate storage mechanism based on the memory type and how the agent needs to access it.

5. Security, Governance, and Guardrails

AI agents interact with external systems and perform actions on behalf of users.

This creates security risks when agents access sensitive information or invoke tools that modify data.

So a production architecture needs security controls at multiple levels:

I) Authentication and authorization

Agents should access only the resources & operations required for their tasks.

A financial analysis agent might need permission to read financial records but should not automatically receive permission to modify them.

The underlying services and tools must enforce authorization, rather than relying solely on instructions provided to the model.

II) Agent-specific guardrails

Guardrails detect/prevent unsafe behaviors:

  • Unauthorized/inappropriate tool execution.

  • Memory poisoning through malicious stored information.

  • Sensitive data exposure across users, agents, or sessions.

  • Prompt injection through untrusted documents or tool responses.

Human approval is another important control for high-risk operations, such as financial transactions or changes to production infrastructure.

A central governance layer lets you define policies and monitor compliance. Yet individual components must enforce the controls relevant to their responsibilities.

A tool gateway should validate permissions before executing an action, while the memory layer should enforce access controls when retrieving stored information.

This architecture establishes how agents execute tasks and interact with external systems.

The next challenge is understanding what happens during execution.

When an agent produces an “incorrect” result, you need to identify whether the failure originated in its reasoning, tool execution, retrieved context, or an external service.

That’s where end-to-end becomes critical…

Agentic AI Observability Layer

Traditional applications follow predefined execution paths.

AI agents add complexity because their decisions, tool calls, and execution paths can vary from run to run.

Imagine a research agent tasked with analyzing a company’s financial performance:

During one execution, it retrieves an annual report and extracts the required figures. During another, it might search many sources, retry a failed API call, or delegate the analysis to another agent.

Both executions would produce the same answer, but their latency, resource usage, and costs differ.

So you need end-to-end observability to understand what happens inside each agent execution.

This visibility offers these capabilities:

  • Track the complete execution path across user requests, agent decisions, model invocations, tool calls, and external services.

  • Identify the source of errors, incorrect outputs, latency spikes, or unexpected costs. Traces provide diagnostic evidence, while evaluations allow assessing response quality.

  • Auditability and governance: Record execution history, policy decisions, guardrail outcomes, and resource usage. Durable audit records with appropriate integrity controls support compliance and accountability.

  • Use execution data and evaluation results to identify inefficient workflows, improve prompts, refine agent logic, and measure the impact of changes.

If an agent takes 30 seconds to complete a task, a distributed trace could reveal 20 seconds were spent waiting for an external API.

You could then optimize the slow dependency instead of changing the model or rewriting the agent’s reasoning logic.

But observability should begin before an agent reaches production.

Build-Time vs Runtime Observability

Agentic AI systems require visibility during development and production lifecycle.

1. Build-Time Observability

Build-time observability focuses on examining system behavior during development, testing, and pre-deployment validation.

It combines telemetry from test executions with evaluation results and system configuration checks.

  • Test whether agents complete expected tasks using predefined datasets and success criteria.

  • Verify that agents select correct tools, provide valid parameters, and handle failures.

  • Measure latency, token consumption, and resource usage under representative workloads.

  • Test access controls, guardrails, and resistance to prompt injection or unauthorized tool execution.

You could run a research agent against 100 predefined tasks and measure its task completion rate, tool call accuracy, and average execution cost.

These results establish a baseline before deployment.

Yet passing pre-deployment tests does not guarantee reliable behavior in production.

Runtime observability tracks how agents behave during actual execution.

It relies on three core telemetry signals:

  • Record discrete events such as tool failures, policy decisions, and execution errors.

  • Measure numerical indicators such as request latency, token consumption, error rates, and cost per task.

  • Connect operations across agents, models, tools, and external services to reconstruct execution paths.

These signals let you investigate failures and monitor production performance.

An agent could repeatedly invoke the same tool without making progress. A trace would reveal the repeated calls, while metrics could show the resulting increase in latency and token consumption.

This matters because agent behavior could change based on user inputs, retrieved information, and intermediate tool results.

Runtime monitoring lets you identify these risks:

  • The agent gradually deviates from the original task.

  • Repeated reasoning or tool calls prevent the workflow from completing.

  • Unexpected tool execution: The agent invokes unnecessary or inappropriate operations.

  • Excessive model calls or retries consume more resources than expected.

Observability detects and investigates these behaviors.

Enforcing execution limits, permissions, and safety policies requires extra controls within the agent architecture.

Build-time evaluation establishes expected behavior. Runtime observability reveals how the agent performs under real workloads. Thus providing the evidence needed to improve agent reliability and operational efficiency.

The next step is to connect these observations across distributed components.

OpenTelemetry collects and correlates telemetry from agent executions, model invocations, and tool calls.

OpenTelemetry for AI Agent Observability

When an AI agent executes a task, it could invoke multiple models, call external tools, and delegate work to other agents.

Each operation generates telemetry.

But without a common way to connect these events, identifying the cause of a failure becomes hard.

OpenTelemetry () provides a vendor-neutral framework for collecting and exporting traces, metrics, and logs across distributed systems.

Distributed tracing lets you reconstruct a task's execution path and understand where time and resources were spent in agentic AI.

1. Core Tracing Principles

Before instrumenting an agentic system, you need a consistent approach to tracing operations across components.

Here are four principles to establish the foundation:

  • Standardized trace propagation: Use the World Wide Web Consortium () Trace Context standard to propagate tracing information across services.

  • One task, multiple spans: Represent an AI task with a trace. Each model invocation, tool call, or agent operation becomes a span. Record retries as separate operations to preserve their execution history.

  • Span links for related operations: Use span links to connect operations with non-hierarchical relationships, such as asynchronous jobs or workflows that cross trace boundaries. Parent-child relationships remain appropriate for ordinary parallel operations within a trace.

  • Keep trace and span identifiers free of business meaning. Store task details, agent names, and other contextual information in attributes.

These principles maintain consistent tracing across agent frameworks and external services.

2. Trace Identifiers and Relationships

OpenTelemetry uses traces and spans to represent distributed operations.

A trace represents the execution path of a request/operation. Each span records an individual operation within that trace.

Here are four important identifiers and relationships:

  • Identifies a trace and connects related spans across services.

  • Uniquely identifies a span within its trace.

  • Identifies the parent span, establishing the execution hierarchy.

  • Span links Associate a span with other span contexts, including operations in separate traces.

Imagine an AI research agent that receives a request, retrieves documents, and generates a summary.

The execution could produce the following trace:

Each operation has its own span, while the spans share a common trace ID.

If document retrieval fails, you inspect the corresponding span to identify the error, execution duration, and affected service.

For long-running workflows, a single task could span multiple traces. In such cases, a separate task or workflow identifier correlates executions across trace boundaries.

3. OpenTelemetry Attributes for AI Agents

Trace identifiers show how operations connect.

Span attributes describe what happened during each operation.

For agentic AI systems, here are the categories of useful attributes:

  • Agent name, operation type, execution status, and workflow identifiers.

  • Model provider, model name, token usage, and inference-related information.

  • Tool name, operation details, execution status, and errors.

  • Operation duration, request latency, and other performance measurements.

  • Guardrail outcomes, policy decisions, and relevant audit references.

OpenTelemetry provides Generative AI semantic conventions for several model, agent, and tool operations.

Additional application-specific attributes should be necessary for workflow state, governance, and cost attribution.

Use standardized OpenTelemetry attributes wherever applicable.

Define custom attributes only when existing conventions do not cover required information.

4. Trace Correlation and Auditability

Once you collect the relevant spans and attributes, you can reconstruct an AI task's execution history.

  1. Which agent received the original request.

  2. Which model generated the execution plan.

  3. Where retries, errors, or latency spikes occurred.

  4. Which tools were invoked and whether they succeeded.

  5. How many tokens were consumed during model invocations.

This information lets you identify failures, analyze resource usage, and investigate unexpected agent behavior.

Yet telemetry alone does not guarantee a complete or tamper-proof audit trail. Production systems need proper retention policies, access controls, and integrity protections.

Plus, you must avoid recording sensitive prompts, credentials, or personal information in telemetry unless explicitly required and properly protected.

The next section explores how to turn agent traces and logs into evaluation datasets to measure task success, response quality, and tool utilization.

Agentic Evaluation and Optimization

Observability tells you what happened during an agent’s execution.

Evaluation determines whether the agent performed its task correctly.

A research agent could successfully call every tool and generate a response within two seconds. Yet the response could contain incorrect financial figures or miss crucial information from retrieved documents.

Traditional performance metrics, such as latency and error rates, would not reveal these quality issues. So you need agent-specific evaluations to measure task success, response quality, and tool usage.

Let’s examine key metrics:

Agent efficiency measures how effectively an agent completes its assigned task.

Some metrics evaluate the final response, while others assess intermediate actions and execution behavior.

Task and reasoning quality

  • Measures the percentage of tasks completed according to predefined success criteria. This is one of the most important indicators of agent effectiveness.

  • Evaluates whether the agent’s observable plans and actions align with the user’s request.

  • Asses whether agent’s observable planning steps follow a logical sequence without unnecessary or contradictory actions.

  • Task decomposition efficiency: Measures how effectively an agent divides complex tasks into manageable subtasks, considering dependencies and unnecessary steps.

Reasoning-based metrics require access to explicit plans or other observable reasoning artifacts.

Many “hosted” models do not expose their internal reasoning, so evaluations should focus on available execution evidence.

  • Measures whether response address user’s original request.

  • Evaluates whether claims in the response are supported by the retrieved documents or trusted evidence.

  • Assesses grammar, readability, and natural language quality.

  • Measures whether the response is logically structured and internally consistent.

An agent could produce a fluent financial summary while reporting incorrect revenue figures. Its fluency score might be high, but its groundedness and factual accuracy scores would be low.

Reliability and consistency

  • Measures how reliably an agent handles unexpected inputs, tool failures, and adversarial scenarios.

  • Evaluates whether repeated executions with similar inputs produce results that satisfy the same correctness criteria.

These metrics identify cases where an agent appears successful but produces unreliable outcomes.

2. Tool Utilization Efficiency

AI agents depend on external tools to retrieve information and perform actions.

Choosing the wrong tool, passing invalid parameters, or making unnecessary calls increases latency and cost.

Here are four metrics to evaluate tool usage:

  • Measures how often the agent selects an appropriate tool for the task.

  • Evaluates whether the agent completes its work with a reasonable number of tool calls and minimal unnecessary operations.

  • Measures whether the arguments passed to a tool are valid and appropriate for the requested operation.

  • Measures the percentage of tool invocations that complete successfully.

Imagine a research agent that needs to retrieve a company’s annual report.

The agent could invoke the document search tool five times with different queries before retrieving the correct report.

All five calls might succeed technically, resulting in a 100% tool call success rate. Yet the agent’s tool usage efficiency would be poor because several calls were unnecessary.

To measure these metrics accurately, you need evaluation criteria, expected outcomes, or reference examples. Execution logs alone don't show whether a tool was the best choice.

3. OpenTelemetry-Based Evaluation Architecture

Once you define the evaluation metrics, the next step is to collect execution data and evaluate agent behavior.

OpenTelemetry provides traces, logs, and metrics to reconstruct agent executions across models, tools, and external services.

These telemetry signals could support two evaluation approaches:

Offline evaluation analyzes previously recorded executions or runs agents against predefined test datasets.

An evaluation service retrieves relevant traces and logs, reconstructs the execution history, and calculates quality metrics.

  • Analysis of failed production interactions.

  • Regression testing after prompt/model changes.

  • Identification of recurring tool usage or response quality issues.

  • Comparison of agent versions using the same evaluation dataset.

Offline evaluation does not require evaluation service to run inside live request path.

Online evaluation assesses agent behavior during production execution.

The application or telemetry pipeline sends relevant execution artifacts to an evaluation service. The service then calculates selected metrics and records the results.

You could evaluate a sample of production responses for groundedness and flag low-scoring interactions for further investigation.

Online evaluations run synchronously when immediate validation is required or asynchronously to avoid increasing user-facing latency.

Both approaches rely on evaluation criteria and access to necessary execution artifacts.

4. Offline Evaluation Architecture

The evaluation process follows four steps:

Step 1: Trigger Evaluation

A user or automated workflow initiates an evaluation through the Evaluate API.

The request specifies the evaluation scope:

  • Agent name or identifier.

  • Tool descriptions or relevant tool metadata.

  • Date range for retrieving previous interactions.

  • Selected evaluation metrics, such as tool selection accuracy or answer relevance.

Depending on the selected metrics, the evaluator would require reference answers, expected tool calls, or ground-truth data.

Step 2: Retrieve Agent Interactions

The evaluation service queries the telemetry backend to retrieve agent executions.

OpenTelemetry trace identifiers correlate operations within each execution, including model invocations, tool calls, and errors.

The evaluator reconstructs the available execution history from these records. It retrieves the model response, selected tool, tool arguments, and execution outcome for a specific research task.

The required data must have been captured during execution. Standard telemetry does not automatically contain every prompt, response, or evaluation artifact.

Step 3: Evaluate Agent Performance

The evaluation engine analyzes retrieved interactions using selected evaluation methods.

One approach is , where a language model evaluates an agent’s output against predefined criteria.

The evaluator assesses whether a generated financial summary accurately reflects the retrieved annual report. Other metrics could use deterministic checks, reference answers, or direct comparisons with expected tool calls.

The evaluation engine then generates:

  • A score for each selected metric.

  • Supporting evidence for the result.

  • An overall evaluation result, where applicable.

The results are stored in persistent storage, such as object or Blob storage, for later analysis.

LLM-based scores should be validated against human-reviewed examples to assess their reliability.

Step 4: Publish Evaluation Results

Users retrieve evaluation results through these APIs:

  • Returns a summary of evaluation runs, including their status and aggregate scores.

  • Returns detailed scores, supporting evidence, and explanations for individual interactions and metrics.

These results let you compare agent versions, investigate failures, and identify improvement opportunities.

If a new prompt increases task success but doubles the average number of tool calls, you can compare the quality improvement against the added cost.

Once you understand how effectively an agent performs its tasks, the next question is how much each execution costs.

This brings us to FinOps for agentic AI systems.

-

Running AI agents in production creates costs beyond individual model requests.

An agent might invoke a language model several times, retrieve documents from a vector database, call external APIs, and delegate tasks to other agents before producing a final response.

Each operation consumes resources.

FinOps lets you understand these costs and make informed decisions about infrastructure, model selection, and resource allocation.

For agentic AI systems, the goal is to measure the cost of each execution and optimize spending without compromising task quality or reliability.

OpenTelemetry () provides execution data that links resource consumption to individual agent workflows.

items.title: Infrastructure as Code - A Deep Dive
items.author: Ayaan
items.content:
We’ve all created infrastructure manually at some point.

A few clicks in a cloud console, some configuration changes, and our servers, networks & databases are up and running.

Sounds simple enough, right?

But what if you need to recreate the same infrastructure for another environment? You’ll have to go through all those settings & reconfigure the resources. Then you’ll need to set up their dependencies and make sure that everything matches the original environment.

And if you miss even one setting, you could spend hours figuring out why something works in staging but fails in production.

Now imagine managing hundreds of resources across multiple environments…

Different engineers are changing these resources regularly. Keeping track of everything manually would become a headache…!

You could use scripts to automate some of this work.

But scripts need to handle resources already running. They must account for changes to existing configurations and failures along the way.

Wouldn’t it be easier if you could write down how our infrastructure should look? You could keep it in Git and let a tool figure out what needs to change whenever you update it.

Well, this is the basic idea behind Infrastructure as Code ()… And Terraform is one of the most widely used tools for managing infrastructure this way.

With Terraform, you define infrastructure using configuration files.

You preview changes before applying them and manage existing resources without repeating every step manually.

But have you ever wondered how Terraform knows which resources already exist? And how it decides what needs updating and what should be created first?

Your coding agent can already paste a Mermaid chart into a PR description.

You still read every file to learn what it does to your system.

draws each pull request as a live architecture canvas, right in your pull request. Press play and it walks you through the change, one step at a time.

  • , marked on the parts of the system it touches

  • , including services the diff never names

  • through the system now

  • , flagged before you merge

2,200+ GitHub stars and 45,000+ pull requests drawn.

(Thanks to Coldtea for partnering on this newsletter.)

I want to introduce as a guest author.

He’s a Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) who writes about Kubernetes, cloud infrastructure, and cloud-native systems. He builds in public and shares practical tips, projects, and lessons learned along the way.

Check out his work & socials:

  • How Terraform turns a few lines of configuration into real cloud infrastructure, and what happens behind the scenes.

  • The architecture behind Terraform: how Terraform Core, providers, and backends work together to manage infrastructure.

  • How Terraform knows which resources already exist, what needs to change, and which resources to create first.

  • How to stop managing infrastructure manually and start using state, dependency graphs, and reusable modules to manage changes.

  • What really happens when you run , and why a failed deployment doesn’t automatically roll back.

  • How to detect configuration drift, import existing infrastructure, and prevent unexpected resource replacements.

  • How to safely manage Terraform in production with CI/CD pipelines, state locking, plan reviews, and access controls.

What Is Infrastructure as Code

IaC is a way to create & manage infrastructure through configuration files.

Instead of setting up resources manually, you define them in files and use those files to manage the infrastructure.

A file could describe a network, a subnet within it, a server connected to the subnet, and the rules that control access. These details stay in Git, making changes visible before they reach the cloud. The configuration remains useful after deployment. It describes what should continue to exist.

There are two main approaches to managing infrastructure through code: imperative and declarative…

The difference lies in how you tell the system what to do.

Imperative vs Declarative Infrastructure

The focuses on to create infrastructure:

You write a series of instructions explaining each step & order in which they should run. A script could first create a network, save its ID, create a subnet inside it, and finally launch a server… The script follows these instructions in sequence.

But what happens if you run the same script again?

It needs extra checks to avoid creating duplicate resources. You also need to handle situations where some steps succeed while others fail.

The works differently:

Instead of writing instructions for every step, you describe the final infrastructure should look like.

Consider a setup where you define a network, a subnet within it, and a server connected to that subnet. Terraform uses these relationships to determine the execution order. Plus, it checks the existing infrastructure to determine which changes are necessary.

The main difference is simple:

Imperative tells the system how to do something, while declarative describes the desired final state.

What Infrastructure as Code Changes

Once the infrastructure is defined in files, changes start with a pull request instead of a series of console clicks.

You review & check the proposed edit before it reaches production. Git keeps a history of the configuration. The same files also help recreate development, staging, or replacement environments with different values.

Mistakes are still possible…

Someone could change resources directly in the cloud console. Also they could approve a configuration with incorrect settings. But the written definition provides a clear reference. It lets you compare intended infrastructure with what actually exists.

Terraform uses this description to plan which resources to create, update, or remove.

Now, let’s look at how Terraform uses this approach to manage real infrastructure…

Terraform as an Infrastructure as Code Tool

Terraform uses a declarative approach:

It helps manage infrastructure across different cloud platforms & services. The same workflow works for networks, databases, and DNS records. It works even when these resources belong to different platforms.

You define the infrastructure using HashiCorp Configuration Language (). Terraform reads these files to understand which resources should exist and how they connect.

Providers then handle platform-specific operations.

A Terraform configuration consists of plain text .

Terraform reads all files in the same working directory as one configuration.

You could keep network resources in one file and servers in another to organize the setup. The file structure makes the configuration easier to manage. But it does not control the order in which Terraform creates resources.

Instead, Terraform follows the relationships between resources.

A server could reference a subnet defined in another file. You don’t need to copy its ID manually. Also HCL supports expressions & conditional values for configurations that need different settings.

Resources are Terraform's main building blocks.

Each resource represents an object Terraform manages, such as a virtual machine or DNS record.

Providers connect Terraform to the platforms where these objects exist. They define which resource types are available. They also handle operations such as creating, updating, and/or deleting those resources.

Other components serve different purposes…Data sources read information about existing infrastructure without taking ownership of those objects.

Variables let you pass values into a configuration, while locals help reuse values within it. Outputs expose useful information, such as a server’s IP address. Modules group related resources into reusable configurations. i.e., you don’t have to repeat the same setup.

Terraform also provides meta-arguments to control how resources get created and connected.

and create multiple instances of a resource. Meanwhile, defines dependencies Terraform cannot identify through references.

Configuration, State, and Real Infrastructure

A resource block alone does not give Terraform enough information to manage infrastructure… The configuration describes what should exist.

But Terraform also needs to know which real objects it already manages.

The state tracks which resource addresses in the configuration belong to which objects on the remote platform. Providers read those objects to determine their current condition.

Terraform uses this information to decide what happens to each resource. It determines whether to create, update, replace, remove, or leave it unchanged.

NOTE: Terraform only checks infrastructure when you run a command. It does not automatically detect & fix every change made outside its configuration.

Let’s look at the components responsible for this process…

Terraform needs more than a configuration file to manage infrastructure.

It needs an engine to plan the work & plugins to communicate with each platform. Plus, it needs a place to keep its state between runs.

These responsibilities belong to Terraform Core, provider plugins & backend.

Terraform Core is the engine behind the terraform command.

It reads configuration, evaluates variables & expressions, and loads the existing state. Providers also supply Core with schemas. These describe available resources & settings each resource supports.

With this information, Core determines how resources depend on each other.

Take a subnet as an example: It needs its network to exist first. Meanwhile, Terraform can create unrelated resources at the same time.

Using these relationships, Terraform builds a dependency graph and creates an execution plan. During , Terraform Core coordinates the operations and records their results in state as they succeed.

Terraform Core follows the same general process across different platforms.

But each platform has its own APIs & resource types…

Provider plugins handle these differences.

Providers run as separate processes. They communicate with Terraform Core through a plugin protocol based on gRPC. This allows Core to request information & operations without knowing each platform’s API.

Each provider defines the resources & data sources available for its platform, along with the settings it supports.

During planning, providers help Terraform check existing resources. This determines whether they need an update/replacement. When you run , they communicate with the remote APIs to create, read, update, and/or delete resources.

This way, Terraform Core manages the overall execution. Providers handle platform-specific operations.

Terraform needs to remember which resources it manages after a run ends.

The backend determines where Terraform stores this state and how it accesses it.

By default, the local backend saves state on the machine running Terraform. For shared infrastructure, a remote backend allows many engineers and CI/CD pipelines to access the same state.

Some backends also support state locking. It ensures that only one Terraform run can modify the state at a time.

Features such as encryption, backups & version history depend on the storage service.

But storing state remotely doesn’t mean Terraform runs remotely. The command could still run on a laptop or in a pipeline unless you configure remote execution separately.

So providers communicate with the actual infrastructure. Meanwhile, the backend stores the state Terraform uses to track those resources.

To understand this better, let’s look at why Terraform needs state and how it uses it to keep track of infrastructure...

Why Terraform Needs State

Terraform needs to recognize the infrastructure from earlier runs.

This includes resources it created & those it started managing.

To understand this, you could define an EC2 instance as in our configuration. But AWS identifies the actual instance using a unique ID. Terraform stores this connection in state so it knows which EC2 instance belongs to the resource defined in our files.

Resource Identity and State Data

State stores more than resource IDs.

It contains attributes returned by providers & output values. Terraform uses this information to track resources inside modules. When you use or to create multiple resource instances, Terraform tracks each one separately.

This information becomes crucial when you modify the configuration.

Consider what happens when you remove a resource block. The actual resource is not immediately deleted from the cloud.

Terraform still has a state entry that identifies the remote object associated with the removed block. During , it uses this information to determine which resource to delete.

Local State vs Remote State

By default, Terraform stores state in a local file.

This works well for learning or managing a small project alone.

But things get more complicated when many engineers or CI/CD pipelines work on the same infrastructure. If everyone maintains a separate copy, one person could make changes without the others having the latest state.

A remote backend solves this problem by providing authorized Terraform runs with access to a shared state file. Depending on the storage service, it also offers better access control and recovery.

Moving state to a remote backend only changes where Terraform stores its records. The actual servers, networks, and other infrastructure remain where they are.

State Locking and Security

When many Terraform runs access same state, there’s a risk of conflicting changes.

To prevent this, supported backends provide state locking. Terraform locks the state when needed, which prevents other runs from modifying it at the same time.

State also needs proper security because it can contain sensitive information. Terraform hides these values from command output, but they still remain in the state file.

For production environments, a few precautions are important:

  • Restrict access to state files.

  • Keep state files & saved plans out of Git.

  • Enable encryption, backups & versioning in the storage service.

  • Avoid the force-unlocking state unless the original operation has ended.

The file is different from the state file.

It records the selected provider versions and checksums, so it normally belongs in Git.

Along with tracking existing resources, Terraform needs to understand how they depend on each other. It uses these relationships to determine how to make changes.

How Terraform Understands Resource Dependencies

Infrastructure resources often depend on one another.

A subnet needs a Virtual Private Cloud () to exist before it gets created, while other resources require specific permissions or settings to be in place.

Terraform identifies these relationships as dependencies. It then uses them to decide the order in which resources should be managed.

Most dependencies get identified through references in the configuration.

When creating a subnet inside a VPC, you need to specify which VPC it belongs to. Instead of manually entering the VPC ID, you reference in the subnet’s setting.

Terraform uses this reference to understand which VPC the subnet belongs to. First, it creates the VPC & then proceeds with the subnet.

The resources don’t need to be defined in the same either. Terraform follows their relationships regardless of how the configuration files are organized.

Not every dependency involves referencing another resource’s value.

An EC2 instance may need an IAM policy attachment completed before its application starts. Yet the instance configuration does not necessarily reference the attachment directly.

In such cases, you use to declare the dependency explicitly. Terraform then waits for the required operation to finish before proceeding.

You should avoid using unnecessarily…Resources could end up waiting for each other, even when Terraform could create them in parallel.

Terraform brings these relationships together in a dependency graph.

This helps it decide which resources to create first.

If a VPC must exist before a subnet is created, the VPC gets processed first. Meanwhile, independent resources could be created in parallel because they don’t rely on each other.

Yet a circular dependency creates a problem. If two resources depend on each other, neither has a valid starting point, so Terraform reports an error instead of proceeding.

During destruction, the order reverses. Dependent resources get removed before the infrastructure they rely on.

Terraform uses these dependencies to order the changes in a plan.

Now, let’s look at what happens to each resource throughout its lifecycle.

  • How real-world systems handle scale, reliability & performance.

items.title: High Performance LLM Inference
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
We were taught that making LLM inference faster means using more powerful GPUs.

That advice is exactly why we have expensive hardware underused while users wait longer for responses.

Here’s what works instead:

It works toward a goal and can act through tools like Gmail or Slack. You can also give it n8n workflows as tools that run exactly as you built them, so you decide which actions the agent handles on its own and which follow a set process. Add approvals before sensitive actions and see every action it takes.

Built for teams that need agents they can rely on.

(Thanks to n8n for partnering on this newsletter.)

Batching processes many requests together instead of running each request through the model separately.

A real AI service might have many users waiting for tokens at the same time. Processing each request separately would leave much of the GPU’s available capacity unused.

Batching allows several sequences to be processed together.

During decode, the GPU repeatedly needs access to the model’s weights. When only one request is being processed, those weights are being used to advance only one sequence.

Imagine four users are waiting for their next token:

The inference system groups those requests into a “batch”.

During the next decode step, the GPU processes the current position for ALL four sequences together. The model weights are still needed, but the work done with those weights is spread across several requests. This gives the GPU more computation to perform for the data it accesses and makes better use of its parallel processing capacity.

The same idea applies to arithmetic intensity.

Processing more sequences together increases the amount of useful computation performed while the model weights are being used. But batching does not make additional requests free.

A batch of thirty-two requests requires more computation than a single request.

Each sequence also has its own attention work, intermediate values, and KV cache. As the batch grows, both compute & memory usage increase. The advantage is the GPU can use its resources much more efficiently.

This introduces an important distinction between latency & throughput.

  • Latency describes how long an individual request takes.

  • Throughput describes how much total work the system can complete in a time period, typically measured in tokens per second across all requests.

Batching mainly improves throughput because the system advances many sequences together instead of one at a time.

But there are limits to how large a batch could become…Memory is one of them.

Every active request needs space for its KV cache, and the cache grows as the sequence gets longer. A large batch of long conversations could eventually consume the available GPU memory.

Timing creates another problem…

Real requests do not arrive/finish together.

Imagine four requests enter a batch:

Request A → finishes after 20 tokensRequest B → finishes after 100 tokens

Request C → finishes after 50 tokens

Request D → finishes after 200 tokens

Request A finishes much earlier than Request D.

With “static” batching, the group gets formed before processing begins. When shorter requests finish, their places are not immediately filled with new requests. So newer requests wait while the remaining requests in the current batch continue.

This reduces some of the efficiency batching was meant to provide.

Real traffic is constantly changing…

  • Users send prompts at different times.

  • Plus prompts have different lengths.

  • Also generated answers finish after different numbers of tokens.

i.e., an efficient serving system needs a batch that changes while the model is generating.

That’s why we need continuous batching...

Continuous batching means changing the group of requests being processed as requests finish & new ones become ready.

Imagine 32 requests starting together:

One request finishes after 20 tokens, another after 100, and another keeps generating for 500 tokens.

With static batching, the group gets decided before generation begins. Shorter requests finish while longer ones are still running. New requests then have to wait for the current batch to complete.

Continuous batching changes how the system schedules this work. (Remember, decode happens one step at a time.)

The model generates the next token for the active sequences, then moves to the next generation step. Instead of scheduling an entire request from beginning to end, the system makes scheduling decisions between these iterations.

This is called “iteration-level” scheduling.

Suppose the active batch looks like this:

After a generation step, Request A finishes.

The scheduler removes A and uses the available capacity for another waiting request when the system has enough compute and memory available.

The batch can therefore change while generation continues.

Step 1 → A B C DStep 2 → A B C D

i.e., the system does not need to wait for B, C & D to finish before it considers E.

This makes continuous batching better suited to real traffic, where requests arrive at different times and generate answers of different lengths. The idea became important in LLM serving through systems such as Orca, which introduced iteration-level scheduling for generative Transformer models. Modern inference engines such as vLLM use continuous batching as part of their serving systems.

But adding a new request is not free/automatic.

Every active request consumes resources, including space for its KV cache. Also, the scheduler has a limit on how many sequences and tokens it can process in one iteration. A new request only joins when the system has enough capacity to schedule its work.

Besides new requests need prefill before they continue through decode.

Modern inference engines must decide how to schedule prefill work alongside requests already generating tokens.

So continuous batching is about more than filling empty slots…

The scheduler repeatedly decides which requests should use the GPU next instead of locking the GPU into one batch until every request finishes. This keeps the hardware busy even when users arrive & leave at unpredictable times.

Plus different requests could share more than the same GPU.

Many begin with the same tokens. Recomputing those tokens every time creates another unnecessary workload.

This is where you need prefix caching...

Prefix caching means reusing the KV cache for a prompt beginning the model has already processed.

Many requests sent to an AI app begin with the same tokens.

  • A chatbot would use the same system instructions at the beginning of every request.

  • A Retrieval-Augmented Generation () application would repeatedly send the same document/context before asking different questions about it.

Even a normal multi-turn conversation contains repeated text.

When you send another message, the app sends much of the earlier conversation back to the model as part of the new prompt. Without caching, the model would process those repeated tokens again during prefill.

But the KV cache could help.

During prefill, the model computes keys & values for prompt tokens and stores them in the KV cache.

If another request begins with exactly the same sequence of tokens, the system reuses the keys and values already computed for that shared beginning.

That shared beginning is called a “prefix”.

Imagine 2 requests look like this:

Request A: [System instructions] + [Document] + “Summarize this”

Request B: [System instructions] + [Document] + “What are the main arguments?”

Both requests begin with same system instructions & document.

With prefix caching, the inference system reuses cached KV data for the matching prefix instead of recomputing it. Prefill only needs to process the part that is not already available in the cache.

The keyword here is .

The matching tokens have to appear at the beginning of the request. Once the token sequence differs, later KV states depend on that different sequence and cannot simply be reused as part of the same cached prefix.

This is why prompt order matters for caching.

If an app has a large block of instructions/context that stays the same across requests, placing that stable content before the parts that change increases how much of the prompt is reusable.

Prefix caching reduces repeated prefill computation.

For long shared prefixes, this reduces time to first token because the model has fewer uncached prompt tokens to process before generation begins. Also it reduces cost when a provider charges for cached input tokens than for uncached input tokens.

But a cached prefix does NOT make the entire request free.

Any new part of the prompt still needs processing, and output still has to go through decode.

Now many requests share the GPU, batches change while generation runs, and cached prefixes avoid repeated work.

But when more requests are waiting than the system can handle at once, the request scheduler decides which one runs next…

Request scheduling decides which requests get to use the model & when they get to run.

Continuous batching lets requests enter & leave while generation is happening.

But the GPU can only handle so much work at once…

Imagine 100 requests waiting, but the inference server currently has enough capacity to process only part of them…The remaining requests have to wait. This creates a “queue”. The scheduler sits between that queue & the model. Its job is to decide which requests move from waiting into active processing.

The simplest approach is first-come-first-served ():

  • The first request to arrive is considered first.

  • If Request A arrives before Request B, the scheduler tries to process A before B.

But arrival time is not the only way to make this decision…

Some systems also support priority scheduling. A request can be assigned a priority, and the scheduler considers higher-priority work before lower-priority work. Arrival time can then decide between requests with the same priority.

Choosing a request is only part of the scheduler’s job.

Also it has to check whether enough resources are available to run it. Every active request needs KV-cache memory, and the model also has a limit on how many sequences & tokens it can process during an iteration.

So even if a request is next in the queue, the scheduler cannot keep adding work.

Suppose the GPU is already processing several long conversations:

Their KV caches occupy most of the available cache memory. Another request is waiting... Before admitting it, the serving system has to check whether enough capacity remains.

Admitting too many requests could create memory pressure and force the system to interrupt and/or rearrange already running work.

“Admission control” decides whether new work should enter the active system based on currently available resources. The exact rules depend on the inference engine, but the goal is the same: avoid accepting more active work than the system can handle efficiently.

Scheduling therefore involves more than asking,

The system has to balance waiting requests against available compute, token budgets & KV-cache memory.

This matters even more because the KV cache is NOT a fixed size.

Every new token makes it grow. With many active users, those caches have to share a limited amount of GPU memory. How that memory is allocated determines how many requests the server can keep running at once.

That brings us to PagedAttention…

PagedAttention is a technique that manages the KV cache in small blocks instead of storing each request’s cache in one large, continuous area of GPU memory.

KV cache grows as a model processes more tokens... The problem is the inference server does NOT know exactly how large each request’s KV cache will become…

Imagine a user sends a prompt & model is allowed to generate up to 1,000 tokens:

The answer might finish after 100 tokens, or it might use almost the entire limit. One approach is to reserve enough continuous GPU memory for the maximum possible sequence length before generation begins.

But much of that reserved space could remain unused if the request finishes early.

There is another problem called “fragmentation”.

Imagine GPU memory as a row of storage spaces:

Requests enter & leave, creating free spaces in different places over time. There may be enough free memory in total for a new KV cache, but not enough “continuous” free space where the system expects to place it.

Both problems waste memory that could otherwise hold more active requests.

PagedAttention solves this by borrowing an idea from operating-system virtual memory: .

Instead of requiring a request's KV cache to occupy one continuous area of physical memory, PagedAttention divides it into “fixed-size” blocks.

A request then uses blocks located in different places in GPU memory.

The blocks do not have to sit next to each other physically.

The system tracks their locations using a “block table”. This gives the model a logical view of the request’s KV cache while the memory manager handles where those blocks actually live.

Also more blocks could be allocated as the sequence grows…

Instead of reserving memory for a 1,000-token answer that might stop after 100 tokens, the system allocates KV-cache blocks as they’re needed.

Some space may remain in the final block.

A sequence does not always end exactly at a block boundary. But the amount of wasted memory is much smaller than reserving a large continuous region for every request.

This matters because KV-cache memory limits how many requests remain active on a GPU.

If each request wastes less memory, the server could keep more sequences in memory at the same time. This enables larger effective batches, thus increasing throughput.

Plus, paged blocks make sharing KV-cache data easier.

If two requests share the same cached prefix, their block tables refer to the same physical KV-cache blocks instead of storing another copy for each request. (This connects PagedAttention directly to the prefix caching.)

The original vLLM work reported near-zero waste in KV-cache memory. Also it improved throughput two to four times over the serving systems it compared against while maintaining similar latency.

PagedAttention does not make the KV cache smaller by changing what the model stores. Instead, it changes how that cache is placed and managed in memory, thus allowing the available GPU memory to be used more efficiently.

But KV-cache storage is only one part of the attention problem.

Even with efficient memory allocation, the model has to perform the attention computation itself.

This brings us to FlashAttention…

FlashAttention is a faster way to compute attention by how much data moves between different GPU memory levels.

When the model processes a sequence, each token needs a way to decide which earlier tokens are relevant. Attention does this by comparing tokens & producing scores that describe how strongly one position should attend to another.

For a sequence with 2,000 tokens, this could involve millions of attention scores.

A straightforward implementation creates a large matrix containing these intermediate scores.

The GPU writes intermediate data to its high-bandwidth memory (), reads it back for another operation, writes another result, and continues through the attention calculation.

The calculations themselves are fast on a GPU.

But moving all those intermediate values between HBM & GPU’s much smaller on-chip memory would become extremely expensive.

FlashAttention changes how this calculation is performed.

Instead of computing & storing the entire attention matrix in HBM, it divides the work into smaller pieces called “tiles”. Each tile is small enough for the GPU to work on using its faster on-chip SRAM.

The GPU loads a portion of the required data, performs several parts of the attention calculation there, and combines the results without writing the full attention matrix to HBM.

This keeps more of the work close to the GPU’s compute units.

Instead of repeatedly moving large amounts of intermediate data in and out of HBM, FlashAttention reduces these expensive memory transfers.

There is an important detail here:

FlashAttention does not approximate standard attention to make it faster. It computes exact attention while changing how the computation is organized around the GPU’s memory hierarchy.

Also it does not remove the quadratic amount of arithmetic required by standard dense attention.

If the sequence length doubles, the number of token-to-token comparisons still grows roughly with the square of the sequence length. FlashAttention reduces the intermediate memory it needs and the number of expensive reads and writes to HBM.

Its auxiliary memory requirement grows linearly, not quadratically, with sequence length.

This distinction explains why FlashAttention makes exact attention much faster without changing what the attention operation computes.

The original FlashAttention work showed that paying attention to where data moves, not only how many calculations are performed, produces large speed improvements.

PagedAttention & FlashAttention therefore solve two different memory problems:

  • PagedAttention manages how the KV cache gets stored while serving requests.

  • FlashAttention improves how the attention calculation itself moves data through GPU memory.

But even an efficient algorithm still has to become instructions the GPU can execute.

Those instructions run inside GPU kernels…

  • Deep dive into how popular real-world systems work.

  • How real-world systems handle scale, reliability & performance.
