items.title: System Design Interview: Design Live Streaming System
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
50 million people hit play, and your live streaming system has only a few seconds to respond…!

A live streaming platform must capture a high-quality video feed, process it in near real time, and deliver it to millions of viewers across phones, laptops & TVs.

Traffic could surge within seconds when a match starts/key moment occurs.

Every stage adds latency, and every bottleneck puts the stream at risk.

In this newsletter, we’ll break down the system design of a live streaming platform built for 50 million viewers.

Let’s start with the system requirements…

Every agent PR comes with a screenshot. Agents open them faster than anyone can read them.

adds the architecture. It draws each pull request as a canvas of your system, marks every part new, changed, or removed, and walks you through how it fits.

  • , marked on the parts of the system it touches

  • , including services the diff never names

  • through the system now

  • , flagged before you merge

2,200+ GitHub stars and 45,000+ pull requests drawn.

(Thanks to Coldtea for partnering on this newsletter.)

He’s an author, educator, and software engineer with a strong passion for building simple, scalable systems.

He authored the O’Reilly book “System Design on AWS” and is working on the upcoming O’Reilly book “System Design From Scratch”. He also supports others’ learning and development by sharing lessons on Cloud and System Design on YouTube.

Before you design the architecture, you must define what the system supports.

i.e., separate functional requirements from non-functional requirements

Functional requirements describe what viewers can do, while non-functional requirements define how well the system must perform at scale.

Functional and Non-Functional Requirements

Here are the key “functional” requirements:

  • Viewers can watch live matches.

  • Video must be streamed based on device type & network bandwidth.

Let’s these features to limit the scope:

  • Multiple audio languages (keep only English),

  • Live chat & user reactions,

“Non-functional” requirements define how well the platform must perform. Here’s an essential list for smooth operations:

  • Low latency: the stream should reach viewers in real time without buffering. For this design, we’ll target 4 to 30 seconds of end-to-end latency.

  • Scalability: traffic could exponentially rise/fall sharply during a live event; the system must absorb sudden spikes in concurrent viewers.

  • Extensibility: architecture should support new event types & device types without major redesigns.

End-to-end latency comes from several stages between capture & playback.

(We’ll examine those stages separately later & see where each one adds delay.)

Latency is only half the problem… Scale also drives many architecture choices…

So let’s put some numbers behind it…

Live events create sharp traffic spikes…

i.e., peak concurrent viewers matter more than average traffic.

  • Maximum concurrent viewers: 50 million

  • Average stream bitrate: 5 Mbps

( is the amount of video data transferred each second.)

So the total outgoing bandwidth for a 1080p video is:

Total Bandwidth = Peak Viewers × Average Bitrate

50,000,000 × 5 Mbps = 250,000,000 Mbps = 250 Tbps

This massive number shows why a central server cannot efficiently deliver the stream to every viewer.

You need video compression, adaptive bitrate streaming, and a Content Delivery Network () to distribute the traffic across edge locations closer to viewers.

Let’s move on to the high-level architecture…

The system streams video from cameras at the event venue to users’ screens.

There are three main phases:

  • Video creation/ingestion,

Here’s the high-level workflow:

  1. High-resolution cameras record the video at the event venue.

  2. The system ingests the video at the venue and prepares it for transfer to application servers for extra processing.

  3. Video processing prepares the stream to support different device types.

  4. Finally, video distribution delivers the stream to users’ devices.

Each phase addresses a different part of the journey from camera to screen.

Let’s start with video ingestion…

The journey starts with cameras at the live event…

These cameras capture high-quality video and create a large amount of data. Transferring the original video directly for further processing would require significant bandwidth & take more time. So the system first reduces the video size while keeping the quality in check.

A video “encoder” at the event location handles this step.

The event location is typically called the Production Control Room (), although the exact terminology varies by company.

The encoder uses video codecs to compress the video.

Here are the popular options:

  • H.264 - Advanced Video Coding ().

  • H.265 - High Efficiency Video Coding (), the successor to H.264.

Once encoded, the smaller video stream needs to reach a central location for further processing & delivery. This infrastructure could run in the cloud or in your own on-premises data center.

Next comes an important design decision: how do you transfer this live video stream with low latency?

Once the video gets encoded, the system must transfer it from the PCR to a central processing location.

Think of it like uploading a large video file to Google Drive:

The upload takes time, especially for large files. But for live streaming, video must reach the processing servers with minimal delay.

Transferring video over the public internet creates 2 challenges:

  • Variable network conditions: Network congestion & packet loss could delay video delivery.

  • Available bandwidth could fluctuate, especially during peak traffic.

For major live events, a “dedicated” network connection helps address these challenges.

A dedicated connection links the event location to the central processing infrastructure without relying on the public internet. It provides more predictable bandwidth & network performance.

Yet it cannot eliminate every source of delay/failure. Plus, setting up and managing dedicated network links requires significant effort.

Cloud providers offer services to simplify this process:

  • Provides dedicated network connectivity between your infrastructure and AWS.

  • Provides private connectivity between your infrastructure and Microsoft Azure.

Both services help establish more predictable network paths for transferring live video to cloud infrastructure.

But network connectivity is only part of the solution. You also need a protocol to transport a continuous video stream efficiently.

Let’s look at the networking protocols used for live video transfer…

Live video requires a continuous data flow between the event location & central processing servers.

In a typical HTTP request, the client sends a request, receives a response, and completes the exchange. But repeatedly establishing connections for a continuous video stream would introduce unnecessary overhead.

A “persistent” connection helps avoid this problem.

WebSockets might seem like an obvious choice… They support persistent, bidirectional communication between clients and servers.

But WebSockets do not provide built-in media transport features such as video codecs, timestamps, or packet-loss recovery. You’d need to implement additional mechanisms to handle live audio & video reliably.

WebSockets are better suited to features such as live chat & viewer reactions.

For transporting live video, we need protocols designed specifically for media delivery.

Real-Time Messaging Protocol

Real-Time Messaging Protocol () is a protocol designed to transfer audio & video streams with low latency.

(Historically, RTMP supported video delivery from streaming servers to client devices through Adobe Flash Player. But Flash Player reached end of life in December 2020.)

RTMP remains widely used for the first phase of live streaming: transferring video from the event location to ingestion servers.

  1. Client initiates a handshake with the RTMP server.

  2. After the handshake succeeds, the client establishes a persistent connection.

  3. RTMP divides media stream into smaller chunks & transfers them over connection.

  4. The server receives the chunks & reconstructs the media stream for further processing.

RTMP runs over TCP, which provides reliable, ordered data delivery.

Yet TCP introduces a trade-off:

When packets get lost, TCP retransmits them. Subsequent data may be delayed until the missing data arrives, a behavior known as . And this could increase latency or cause playback interruptions under poor network conditions.

A dedicated network connection helps reduce congestion and packet loss, thus making RTMP a practical choice for transporting live video from the event venue.

Another limitation is codec compatibility:

Traditional RTMP implementations primarily support H.264 video, while H.265 support requires newer extensions and compatible software.

Secure Reliable Transport

Secure Reliable Transport () is a protocol designed for low-latency video transport.

SRT runs over UDP. SRT adds reliability mechanisms on top of UDP, including packet-loss detection, selective retransmission, and configurable latency buffers.

Here’s the key difference:

  • Uses TCP to deliver data reliably and in order. Packet loss can delay subsequent data while TCP recovers missing packets.

  • Uses UDP with selective retransmission. It attempts to recover lost packets within a configured latency window and avoids waiting indefinitely for packets that arrive too late.

This makes SRT useful when transferring live video over networks with fluctuating bandwidth or packet loss.

Also RTMP has broad support for existing streaming hardware & software. But SRT support depends on the capabilities of the encoder, decoder, and streaming infrastructure.

Both protocols primarily transport video from the source to the streaming backend.

But delivering video from the backend to of viewers requires a different approach…

HTTP Live Streaming () is a streaming protocol by Apple.

Instead of maintaining a continuous media connection between the streaming server and every viewer, HLS divides encoded video into smaller media segments.

Here’s what a typical HLS workflow looks like:

  1. The encoder continuously produces compressed video.

  2. A packager divides the encoded stream into media segments, typically 2 to 4 seconds long.

  3. The system creates a playlist, called a manifest, containing references to available segments.

  4. The video player downloads the playlist and requests segments over HTTP.

  5. As new segments become available, the player continues downloading them to maintain playback.

The camera does not need to stop recording after each segment. Video capture and encoding continue while the packager creates segments from the incoming stream.

Yet segment duration introduces an important trade-off.

Shorter segments could reduce live-stream latency but increase request overhead & place extra demands on the streaming infrastructure. Longer segments reduce request frequency but increase playback delay.

Low-Latency HLS extends this approach by letting players access partial segments before a segment is complete.

(Netflix uses HLS with 2-second segments for its live streaming architecture.)

HLS also offers broad compatibility with modern playback devices and CDNs.

For our architecture, we can use RTMP/SRT to transport video from the event location to the central processing servers, then use HLS to distribute the processed stream to viewers.

If ultra-low-latency playback becomes a requirement, we should evaluate alternatives such as WebRTC or specialized low-latency delivery protocols. SRT remains a strong option for contribution feeds, but it is not a direct replacement for HLS across millions of consumer devices.

Let’s summarize the first phase of our architecture:

  1. Multiple high-resolution cameras record the event from different angles.

  2. Camera feeds reach the PCR or operations center, where the production system inspects and selects the video streams for further processing.

  3. Encoding and compression: Once the production feed is finalized, video encoders compress it using codecs such as Advanced Video Coding (AVC/H.264) or High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC/H.265). This reduces the bandwidth required for transmission. Encoding can happen on-site with hardware or software encoders, or through cloud-based services. For example, AWS Elemental MediaLive provides live video encoding & processing in the cloud.

  4. The compressed stream travels from the event location to centralized processing infrastructure over a dedicated network connection, using a protocol such as RTMP/SRT.

Choosing Video Segment Size

One final consideration is how the continuous video stream gets divided into segments for downstream processing & delivery.

The segment duration affects several factors:

  • Shorter segments reduce the delay between the live event and viewer playback.

  • Segment boundaries must align with the encoded video structure, and the system needs time to prepare segments for delivery.

  • Smaller segments generate more frequent HTTP requests, increasing request volume across clients, servers, and CDNs.

For conventional HTTP-based live streaming, segment durations range from around 2 to 10 seconds, depending on the configuration.

The appropriate value depends on the event’s latency requirements, encoding configuration, network conditions, and geographic distribution of viewers. Once the video gets transferred to the central servers, the next phase prepares it for playback across different devices and network speeds.

Let’s examine video processing next…

Once the video stream reaches the central server, next step is to prepare it for different devices & network conditions.

A viewer watching on a mobile phone with a slow internet connection has different requirements from someone watching on a 4K television with high-speed broadband.

The system must support both without interrupting playback.

converts the incoming video stream into multiple encoded versions, each with a specific resolution, bitrate, and codec.

Two important parameters determine the output:

  • The amount of video data transmitted per second, typically measured in megabits per second (Mbps). Higher bitrates allow better video quality but require more bandwidth.

  • The number of pixels in each video frame, such as 4K, 1080p, 720p, or 480p. Higher resolutions contain more visual detail but typically require higher bitrates to maintain quality.

For example, an MP4 video could be transcoded into many quality levels:

  • 4K, 1080p, or 720p.

  • 1080p, 720p, or 480p.

  • 480p, 360p, or 144p.

Resolution & bitrate are separate parameters, so each output needs its own bitrate configuration. These versions form an adaptive bitrate () ladder.

The video player then selects the appropriate version based on the viewer’s available bandwidth, device capabilities, and playback conditions.

i.e., someone watching on a fast Wi-Fi connection might receive a 1080p stream. If their connection slows down, player can switch to 720p/480p to reduce buffering.

Managed Services vs Custom Transcoding

At this stage, you must decide whether to build your own transcoding infrastructure or use a managed service.

Cloud providers offer services for video encoding & format conversion.

AWS Elemental MediaConvert converts video files into different formats, resolutions, and bitrates. It’s designed for file-based video processing.

For continuous live streams, AWS Elemental MediaLive is an appropriate managed service because it supports real-time video encoding & transcoding.

The output is a collection of video renditions ready for packaging & distribution.

Video Packaging: HLS and DASH

After transcoding, the system must package the video into a format supported by viewers’ devices.

Here are 2 popular protocols:

  • HTTP Live Streaming (HLS): Widely supported across modern streaming platforms.

  • Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (DASH): An open standard for delivering adaptive video streams over HTTP.

Both support adaptive bitrate streaming, thus allowing video players to switch between quality levels as network conditions change.

HLS is commonly used on Apple devices, while many other players and platforms support DASH. Also HLS works on many non-Apple devices, so the choice depends on player and platform compatibility.

Let’s examine how HLS works…

How HLS Organizes Video Segments

HLS divides the encoded video into smaller media segments and generates playlists that tell the player where to find them.

Each segment is typically stored in one of two formats:

  • MPEG-2 Transport Stream, a traditional HLS segment format.

  • Fragmented MP4, commonly used with modern HLS implementations.

The system also generates two types of playlist files, both using the extension.

The master playlist lists the available video renditions, such as 4K, 1080p & 720p.

Each entry includes required bandwidth, resolution, and codec.

The player uses this information to identify compatible renditions and select an appropriate quality level.

Each rendition has its own media playlist.

This playlist contains an ordered list of video segments, along with their durations and locations.

For a live event, the playlist updates as new segments become available. The player repeatedly fetches the latest playlist & downloads appropriate segments.

This structure allows the player to switch between quality levels during playback without restarting the stream.

The system also needs to store video for later playback.

We can retain both the original ingested video & transcoded outputs.

  • Preserves source material for future processing or re-encoding.

  • Allows viewers to replay the event without requiring the system to transcode it again.

Object storage is a common choice for storing these large video files.

Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) stores the original recordings, transcoded renditions, media segments, and manifests.

We also maintain a metadata store to map each event and video rendition to its corresponding file locations in Amazon S3.

When someone wants to watch a completed event, the system uses this metadata to locate the appropriate video assets.

Digital Rights Management

Live sports content typically comes with strict licensing & distribution requirements.

The platform must protect video streams from unauthorized access & playback.

Digital Rights Management () encrypts video content and requires an authorized player to obtain a valid license before decrypting and playing it.

Here are the popular DRM systems:

  • Supported across Android & many browser-based playback environments.

  • Used across various streaming devices, browsers & television platforms.

  • Apple FairPlay Streaming: Used to protect HLS content on supported Apple devices.

AWS Elemental MediaPackage can package live video into HLS/DASH formats and integrate with DRM systems to encrypt content.

But DRM license issuance and key management require integration with a compatible DRM provider or license service.

This ensures authorized viewers access protected streams through supported players.

From Video Processing to Distribution

Let’s summarize what happens after the live video reaches the central processing servers.

  1. The incoming stream gets converted into multiple resolutions and bitrates to support different devices & network conditions.

  2. Each rendition gets divided into media segments and organized into HLS/DASH manifests.

  3. Original recordings, transcoded video, and metadata get stored for live delivery & future playback.

  4. DRM encryption and license services help restrict playback to authorized viewers.

The processed video is now ready for distribution.

But our system must deliver it to 50 million concurrent viewers without overwhelming the central servers. This is where a Content Delivery Network () becomes essential.

Let’s examine video distribution next…

The video is now encoded, transcoded & packaged.

The next challenge is delivering it to 50 million concurrent viewers.

Sending every video segment directly from the central servers would require enormous bandwidth & put massive pressure on the infrastructure.

A CDN caches video segments at edge locations closer to viewers. When thousands of people in the same region watch a match, they receive the same video segments from a nearby edge server instead of repeatedly requesting them from the origin.

But caching introduces a tradeoff:

Cached content could become stale, while live streaming requires viewers to receive new segments with minimal delay. The system must balance cache efficiency with live-stream freshness.

Live video segments are typically immutable once published. So this makes them suitable for caching, while frequently updated manifests require shorter cache durations.

How CDN Distribution Works

Once the video gets transcoded & packaged, the distribution system makes video segments and manifests available through the CDN.

In a typical CDN architecture, edge servers retrieve content from the origin if it’s not already cached. Subsequent requests for the same segment get then served directly from the edge.

Here’s how the process works:

  1. The processing system generates video segments and HLS/DASH manifests.

  2. Packaged content becomes available on an origin server or object storage service.

  3. When an edge location receives a request for uncached content, it fetches the required segment from the origin or upstream CDN cache.

  4. CDN stores the segment temporarily so nearby viewers can access it without another origin request.

  5. Viewers download the segments from edge locations through Internet Service Providers () or mobile networks.

For live sports, viewer demand concentrates in specific geographic regions.

The distribution system must account for these traffic patterns & ensure sufficient CDN capacity in regions where large audiences are expected.

Here are CDN solutions that support this architecture:

  • delivers content through a globally distributed network of edge locations.

  • A distributed caching & content delivery service.

  • Netflix’s own CDN infrastructure, designed to deliver video efficiently to its viewers.

The goal is to serve video from locations close to viewers while reducing traffic to the central processing infrastructure.

Video Pipeline Coordination

Consider 3 major phases we’ve covered:

    These phases depend on one another…

    The system must receive the incoming video before it can process it. Transcoding begins as encoded video becomes available, and distribution starts as soon as the required segments and manifests are ready.

    For live streaming, these stages operate continuously as a pipeline rather than waiting for the entire event recording to finish.

    But failures can occur at any stage…

    The system might generate the 720p rendition while the 1080p transcoding process fails.

    An helps coordinate the services involved in the pipeline. Its responsibilities include:

    • Ensure ingestion, transcoding, packaging, and distribution happen in the correct order.

    • Detect failed processing tasks & trigger necessary recovery actions.

    • Track which outputs are ready for downstream services.

    • Ensure video segments & manifests become available to CDN as processing progresses.

    If the 1080p rendition fails, the system can attempt recovery while continuing to deliver other available renditions.

    This prevents a failure in one quality level from unnecessarily interrupting the entire live stream.

    Bringing Video Closer to Viewers

    The network path between origin infrastructure & CDN locations affects delivery performance.

    CDN providers use private backbone networks, peering connections, and optimized routing to transfer content efficiently.

    Yet the exact network path depends on the CDN provider and deployment architecture. Traffic does not always travel only over dedicated private connections.

    Once the content reaches an edge server, viewers access it through their ISPs or mobile networks.

    This final delivery path uses the public internet.

    To reduce latency and network congestion, CDN providers place caching infrastructure close to major concentrations of viewers.

    Netflix takes this approach with .

    Its Open Connect Appliances are caching servers that can be deployed inside participating ISP networks. This lets Netflix serve content closer to subscribers while reducing traffic across upstream networks.

    AWS offers a related capability through Amazon CloudFront Embedded Points of Presence ().

    These smaller CDN locations extend content delivery infrastructure deeper into ISP networks, bringing cached content closer to end users.

    Both approaches help reduce the distance video data must travel before reaching viewers.

    For a live event with 50 million concurrent viewers, this distributed architecture is essential for handling traffic without overwhelming the origin servers.

    The CDN delivers the video segments…The next step is understanding how a viewer’s device discovers the stream, selects the appropriate quality & plays video.

    Let’s examine video playback next…

    The player must locate the live stream, select the right video quality & download the segments needed for playback.

    Here’s the end-to-end request workflow:

    1. App/site sends a request to the playback service, along with the event details.

    2. Retrieve the master manifest: Playback service provides the master manifest URL, which the player uses to retrieve the available video quality options.

    3. The player chooses an initial quality level based on the available network bandwidth & device capabilities.

    4. Retrieve the media manifest: The player requests the media manifest for the selected quality. This manifest contains references to video segments available through CDN.

    5. The player downloads the video segments from the CDN, buffers enough data to begin playback, and starts displaying the live stream.

    NOTE: We’ve intentionally excluded services responsible for user authentication and authorization, which control access to specific content. Our focus is on delivering live video to viewers with minimal delay.

    How Adaptive Bitrate Streaming Works

    The viewer’s network conditions could change throughout the event… Someone watching on a mobile device might move from a fast Wi-Fi connection to a cellular network.

    If the player keeps downloading high-bitrate video segments, playback could stall because the network cannot deliver data fast enough.

    The video player continuously monitors factors such as available network throughput and playback buffer levels with adaptive bitrate () streaming. It then uses this information to select an appropriate video rendition.

    • When bandwidth increases: Player switches to a higher-bitrate rendition for better video quality.

    • When bandwidth decreases: The player switches to a lower-bitrate rendition to reduce buffering.

    • When network conditions stabilize: Player continues downloading segments at a suitable quality level.

    These switches typically happen at segment boundaries, allowing the player to change video quality without restarting playback.

    The goal is to maintain smooth playback while delivering the highest practical video quality for each viewer.

    We’ve now covered the complete journey from cameras at the event venue to video playback on viewers’ devices.

    But supporting 50 million concurrent viewers creates extra challenges, especially when traffic increases sharply during a major live event.

    Let’s examine how the architecture handles these situations…

    • Deep dive into how popular real-world systems work.

    • How real-world systems handle scale, reliability & performance.

items.title: How LLM Inference Works
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
You type a question into ChatGPT:

A moment later, the answer starts appearing.

From your side, that is the entire interaction…

But behind the screen, an entire “inference” system has already started working.

And it has 3 HARD problems to solve:

  • How to generate tokens quickly when each step needs access to a huge model?

  • How to serve many users without running out of GPU memory & capacity?

  • How to make responses fast for users without wasting expensive hardware?

To answer those questions, we’ll follow one request from the moment you hit Enter to the moment the answer reaches your screen.

Along the way, we will see how tokenization, prefill, decode, KV cache, batching, memory management, and distributed serving all fit together.

Let’s start with the request itself…

A model goes through two main stages: .

During , the model learns its parameters--weights. It processes large amounts of data & repeatedly adjusts those weights to get better at predicting what comes next. Once a trained model gets deployed, those weights are then typically fixed!

When you send the model a prompt, it does not retrain itself on your question. It uses the weights it already learned to produce a response. This process is called inference.

Training creates the model…Inference runs it.

(This distinction becomes important at scale.)

Training requires enormous computing power, but it occurs during model development. Inference occurs every time someone sends a request. The same trained checkpoint can therefore perform inference again and again for as long as it is being served.

Our request is one of those inference jobs.

But “Why is the sky blue?” cannot be handed directly to the model as a string of English text. It first has to be converted into the representation the model expects.

That begins with tokenization…

A token is a piece of text. Sometimes, it is a complete word, and sometimes it is only part of one. Spaces & punctuation also appear as part of tokens.

Large Language Models () work with tokens, not words.

So our question, “Why is the sky blue?”, could be split like this:

[”Why”, “ is”, “ the”, “ sky”, “ blue”, “?”]

The exact split depends on the tokenizer.

Another model may divide the same sentence differently. Each token maps to an integer in the model’s vocabulary. These integers (token IDs) become the model’s discrete input before it maps them to learned vector representations.

That’s why tokens appear everywhere when you use an LLM.

  • API pricing get typically measured in tokens.

  • Context windows get measured in tokens.

  • Generation speed gets measured in tokens per second.

The tokenizer still needs a method for deciding where to split the text.

One common method is Byte Pair Encoding (). It builds a vocabulary by repeatedly finding common adjacent units & merging them. Frequent patterns could eventually become individual tokens, while less common words often get split into several pieces.

This gives the tokenizer a useful compromise.

It does not need a vocabulary containing every possible word. Plus, it does not have to process normal text one character at a time.

Another tokenization framework you may come across is SentencePiece.

SentencePiece applies algorithms such as BPE/Unigram directly to raw text, including whitespace. This makes it useful for languages where spaces are not reliable word boundaries.

By the end of tokenization, our sentence is no longer just text.

It has become a sequence of token IDs. Before the model processes those tokens, however, we need to consider a limit.

That limit is the context window.

It’s the maximum number of tokens a model works with at one time.

Your visible prompt is not necessarily the only thing taking up this space.

A chat request also contains earlier messages, system instructions, retrieved documents, tool definitions, or other information the application sends to the model. Depending on the model & API, generated output also needs to fit within the applicable sequence or output limits. This is why long conversations eventually need some form of context management.

What happens at the limit depends on the application:

A system could remove older messages, summarize them, retrieve only relevant parts, or reject a request that is too large. The model’s context window should NOT be confused with a permanent memory of everything that has happened in conversation.

Context length matters for another reason: longer prompts require more work.

During attention, the model uses information from different positions in the sequence to understand how the tokens relate to one another. As the sequence grows, the model has more information to process & store. This increases computation and memory requirements, although the exact cost depends on the model architecture and attention implementation.

A larger context window also does not mean the model will use every part equally well.

Information buried in the middle of a long prompt can be harder to retrieve than information closer to the beginning/end.

Our question is tiny by comparison:

Once those tokens are inside the available context, the model begins processing them.

Prefill is the stage where the model processes tokens in your prompt before it starts generating an answer.

LLMs are built from many layers stacked on top of one another.

Each layer takes the representation produced by the previous layer, processes it, and passes a new representation forward. By the time the data reaches final layers, the model has built a richer representation of the prompt.

Inside these layers is a mechanism called .

Attention helps the model decide which earlier tokens are useful when processing the current token. In our question, for example, when the model processes blue, information from sky could be relevant to understanding what the sentence is asking.

LLMs used for text generation normally use causal attention.

Causal attention means a token uses information from earlier positions, but not from positions ahead of it.

This preserves the left-to-right structure needed for predicting the next token. During prefill, however, every token in our prompt already exists: “. The GPU can therefore process work across the prompt positions in rather than waiting for each token to be generated first.

While processing the prompt, attention creates keys & values for each token.

You can think of the key as information used to determine when a token is relevant. The value contains the information the model can retrieve. The model keeps these keys & values in the KV cache.

The KV cache will be useful again during generation.

Storing the keys & values means the model does not need to recompute the same key and value projections for every previous token at every generation step.

(We will look much more closely at the KV cache later.)

Once the prompt has passed through the model, it must decide which token comes next.

The model assigns a raw score to every possible token in its vocabulary. These scores are called . A decoding or sampling strategy uses the logits to select the first output token.

Depending on the strategy, this can mean choosing the strongest candidate or sampling from several likely candidates.

The work done before the first generated token contributes to a metric called Time to First Token ().

TTFT measures the time between sending a request and receiving the first part of the response. Prefill contributes to this delay, but it is not the only source. A request can also spend time traveling over the network, waiting for available GPU capacity, or sitting in a queue while the serving system decides which request should run next.

Once the first output token has been chosen, inference enters a different phase…

Decode is the stage where the model generates a response one token at a time.

Suppose the response begins: “The sky appears blue because...”

The model cannot generate the entire sentence in one shot. It first chooses a token such as ‘’. That token becomes part of the sequence. The model then uses the updated sequence to choose the next token.

This is autoregressive generation.

Each newly generated token depends on the tokens before it.

The process looks roughly like this:

TheThe skyThe sky appears blue

At each decode step, the model still needs information from tokens it has already processed.

Instead of recomputing the keys & values for all previous tokens, it reuses them from the KV cache created during prefill. The model computes the key and value for the newest token and adds them to the cache. It then passes the newest token through its layers and produces another set of logits: scores for the possible next token.

The decoding strategy uses those logits to select the next token.

The selected token joins the sequence, and another decode step begins. This process continues until the model reaches a stopping condition, such as an end-of-sequence token or a configured output limit.

During prefill, ALL prompt tokens are already available, so the hardware can process work across many positions in parallel. During ordinary autoregressive decode, the next token does not exist until the previous one has been selected. This sequential dependency makes output generation behave differently from input processing.

There is also a hardware cost inside this loop.

Every decode step runs through the model’s layers & repeatedly accesses a large set of model weights. For large models, moving this data through GPU memory could become a major bottleneck.

This is where the simple story of “model predicts the next token” starts turning into a system design problem…

Streaming is the process of sending parts of the model’s response to the user while the rest of the response is still being generated.

We have already seen how decode works…

The model generates one token, adds it to the sequence, then generates the next one. Without streaming, the server could wait for the entire decode process to finish before returning the answer.

That would leave you looking at an empty screen while the model generates the full response.

Streaming changes when the output reaches you.

Suppose the model is generating: “The sky appears blue because...”

As parts of the response become available, the server could start sending them back to the application. Your browser then displays the beginning while the model is still generating the rest…

Streaming does not make the model generate tokens faster.

It changes when you receive those tokens. For an interactive application such as a chatbot, this makes the response feel more responsive.

How the response reaches your browser

The server needs a way to keep sending data after the request has started.

One common option is ():

SSE keeps an HTTP connection open so server can continue sending events to the client instead of returning one response and immediately closing the exchange.

The communication moves in one direction: server sends updates & client receives them.

This works well for text generation because most of the response data travels from the server to the client after you send your prompt.

Another option is .

A WebSocket creates a persistent connection where both sides can send data:

This two-way communication is useful when the client needs to keep sending information while receiving results. A real-time voice assistant is one example because the user can continue sending audio while the server sends information back.

There is one more detail between decode & what appears on your screen: .

The server does not have to send every generated token as a separate update. It could collect several tokens and send them together as one chunk.

Tokens 1–3 → send together

The choice affects how the response feels.

Sending smaller chunks more frequently makes the response appear smoother. Grouping more tokens into each chunk reduces some of the overhead from repeatedly sending tiny updates.

So there is a tradeoff between responsiveness & communication overhead.

Our request has now completed the first part of its journey:

Text → Tokens → Prefill → Decode → Stream

We started with:

We have followed it from ordinary text to the response appearing on the screen. For one request, this process is manageable. A production AI service has to repeat it for many users while their requests compete for the same hardware.

This is where inference starts becoming a HARD systems problem.

  • High-level architecture of real-world systems.

  • Deep dive into how popular real-world systems work.

  • How real-world systems handle scale, reliability & performance.

items.title: Everyone is a scalability expert till traffic spikes
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
Once upon a time, there lived a junior software engineer named Michiko.

She worked for a tech company named Hooli.

Although she was bright, she never got promoted.

So she was sad & frustrated…

Until one day, she had the idea to apply for a new job.

And the interviewer asked her 1 simple question:

“How to effectively scale a system?”

But she couldn’t answer it & failed the interview in 5 minutes.

So she went home & studied it to fill the knowledge gap.

Your coding agent can already paste a Mermaid chart into a PR description.

You still read every file to learn what it does to your system.

draws each pull request as a live architecture canvas, right in your pull request. Press play and it walks you through the change, one step at a time.

  • , marked on the parts of the system it touches

  • , including services the diff never names

  • through the system now

  • , flagged before you merge

2,200+ GitHub stars and 45,000+ pull requests drawn.

(Thanks to Coldtea for partnering on this newsletter.)

Michiko failed the interview, so you don’t have to.

And here are 11 must-know scalability techniques for you to ace job interviews:

Vertical scaling gives one machine more power by adding CPU, memory, and/or faster disks.

The app stays the same, but the machine it runs on gets more powerful... Or you move the app to a larger instance.

i.e., you do NOT need to rewrite any code. And vertical scaling is probably the quickest way to handle extra load.

It works well for monoliths & older systems built to run on a machine.

Yet larger machines cost more & all machines have limits.

Plus, if your app relies on a single server, a failure could take the entire app down.

So scale up when you need more capacity quickly. Then consider horizontal scaling before one machine becomes your system’s biggest bottleneck.

Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more machines to share the load.

You run several copies of the app & distribute traffic across them using a load balancer.

i.e., you add machines as traffic grows & remove them when demand drops.

It works well for applications with high/unpredictable traffic.

Yet adding machines creates new challenges:

You need load balancing, coordination between instances & keep shared data consistent.

Horizontal scaling improves “availability” with redundant instances. But if your app stores user sessions locally, requests routed to different instances could lose access to session data.

So before you scale out, you need to decide where your application stores its state.

And that’s why you’d need stateless services...

A stateless service does NOT store client session state between requests.

Every request provides information the server needs - auth token or session ID.

Plus, you don’t store session data on server… instead, you keep it in a shared database, a cache like Redis, or use a signed token like a JSON Web Token ().

i.e., any server could handle a request without relying on the previous one.

This makes it easier to add, remove, or replace servers as traffic patterns change.

Yet the state still needs to live somewhere.

And an external database/cache adds infrastructure, network latency & an extra dependency to manage. Plus, relying on sticky sessions to keep users tied to one server reduces flexibility when servers fail or traffic changes.

So keep session state outside individual app instances when possible. Also, design operations to be “idempotent”.

With stateless services, you could scale individual instances more easily.

But what if those services depend heavily on each other…

That’s where you’d need loose coupling...

Loose coupling = each component depends on others as little as possible.

A change in one component could force you to update several others in a “tightly coupled” system.

Plus, if one service becomes slow/fails, the problem could spread to other services that depend on it.

Loose coupling reduces these dependencies by letting components communicate through well-defined interfaces - APIs/messages. So each component knows what to expect from others without understanding their internal implementation.

This makes it easier to update, deploy, and/or scale components independently.

Yet loose coupling introduces extra complexity:

Requests could travel across many services,,, thus making it HARD to trace & debug failures. Also,splitting a system into many tiny services increases communication overhead & coordination costs.

So use loose coupling when components need to evolve independently - microservices & big apps.

And to organize these components into clear, manageable parts, you need modular architecture…

Modular architecture divides a system into separate modules, with each responsible for a specific function.

You divide the app into modules for authentication, orders, payments, notifications, and so on.

i.e., each module has a clear responsibility & communicates with others through defined interfaces.

The goal is to group functionality that belongs together & keep dependencies between modules . This follows the principle of : each module focuses on one part of the system.

So you update/test payment module without changing the authentication module.

Yet choosing the “wrong module boundaries” creates unnecessary dependencies.

Plus, splitting an app into many modules makes the codebase hard to manage. Also, modules within the same app still share resources & failure risks.

So modularity alone does NOT guarantee independent scaling or failure isolation.

It works well for large applications, modular monoliths & microservice architectures!

But if these modules need to communicate without waiting for each other…you’d need event-driven architecture…

6. Event-driven architecture

Event-driven architecture allows services to communicate by publishing & reacting to events.

A service publishes an event to a message broker instead of calling other services directly.

Imagine a user places an order on an e-commerce website:

The service publishes an event… Then other services consume it independently:

  • service reserves ordered items,

  • service initiates payment processing,

  • service sends an order confirmation when required steps succeed.

service does NOT wait for each consumer to finish processing the event.

i.e., a slow consumer does NOT block others.

This approach works well for workflows when many services need to react to the same event.

Yet event-driven systems create new problems:

Events could arrive late, out of order, or more than once. Plus, different services could temporarily hold different versions of the same data. This is called .

So you need idempotent consumers, reliable event delivery & a way to handle failed operations.

Event-driven architecture helps services scale independently & reduces synchronous dependencies.

But when you need to organize these services without creating a central bottleneck, you’ve got to “avoid” …

7. Shared-nothing architecture

Shared-nothing architecture gives each node its own compute, memory & storage relying on shared resources for processing.

items.title: GitOps Deep Dive: How ArgoCD Works
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
The CI/CD pipeline changed how we deploy software.

It made deployments faster, repeatable, and automated. But once a deployment finishes, the pipeline has no idea what happens inside the cluster afterward.

Someone could edit a Deployment with , apply a hotfix during an incident, or update a resource manually. Those changes bypass Git and the pipeline.

As manual changes increase, the cluster slowly drifts from what gets stored in Git.

At some point, production no longer matches the configuration everyone believes is running. When an issue appears, it becomes difficult to see what changed... Also it becomes difficult to know who changed it or whether the running state still matches the last reviewed configuration.

GitOps solves this by making Git the source of truth for the cluster…not just another step in the deployment process…

An agent continuously compares the live cluster with the desired state stored in Git and reconciles any differences. If someone changes a resource outside Git, ArgoCD detects the drift and brings the cluster back to the expected state.

The CI pipeline still builds, tests, and publishes the application.

But instead of deploying directly to Kubernetes, it updates Git. ArgoCD then handles the deployment and keeps the cluster aligned with the repository.

Right now, you’re your agent’s context engine. You write the rules files, maintain the skills, and paste in the Slack thread it missed.

But hand-curated context goes stale. And when there are conflicting answers, your agent can’t tell which is right. You pay for it in higher token bills and longer reviews.

  • The 8-levels of AI maturity and where teams get stuck

  • How a context engine curates context and resolves conflicts before your agent writes a line of code

  • Live demo: token savings in the same coding task, and use cases beyond code gen

Bonus: 2 open source tools you can use today.

(Thanks to Unblocked for partnering on this newsletter.)

I want to introduce as a guest author.

He’s a Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) who writes about Kubernetes, cloud infrastructure, and cloud-native systems. He builds in public and shares practical tips, projects, and lessons learned along the way.

Check out his work & socials:

  • Your deployment succeeds. Then production starts drifting. How manual Kubernetes changes create configuration drift, why traditional CI/CD pipelines miss them, and how GitOps keeps your cluster aligned with Git.

  • Your CI pipeline no longer needs the keys to Kubernetes. How ArgoCD’s pull-based model changes deployments, where credentials live, and what happens when a system gets compromised.

  • ArgoCD runs a reconciliation loop behind the scenes. How its core components detect changes, compare desired and live states, and use sync policies, self-healing, and hooks to control deployments.

  • One template, hundreds of applications. How ApplicationSets manage deployments across clusters, why repository structure matters, and how Git commits promote releases from development to production.

  • GitOps gets harder when you reach production. How to manage secrets, access control, monitoring, progressive delivery, and disaster recovery, plus the tradeoffs you need to understand before adopting it.

GitOps is an operating model where a Git repository is the single source of truth for everything running in your infrastructure.

Every change to your application or cluster configuration happens through a Git commit. It gets reviewed, approved, and merged through the same process as application code.

i.e., changes are not applied directly to the cluster outside Git.

The OpenGitOps working group at CNCF defined four principles to distinguish GitOps from a traditional deployment pipeline.

In a declarative system, you describe what you want, not how to get there.

Instead of writing a script with steps like “create this deployment, then scale it to three replicas, then expose it on port 80,” you write a YAML file describing the end state. The system figures out how to make it happen.

Kubernetes is declarative by nature.

Helm charts, Kustomize overlays, and raw YAML manifests all follow the same model.

This matters for GitOps because a declarative system supports storage, versioning, and comparison. Unlike a sequence of commands, two YAML files allow you to see exactly what changed.

2. Versioned and Immutable

Every change to the desired state is a Git commit.

And Git commits do not change…

This gives you a complete, tamper-evident history of everything your cluster has ever been asked to run. Who requested the change, who approved it, when it got merged, and exactly what it modified. The audit trail becomes part of the deployment workflow, not a separate system.

Rollback is also a natural consequence of this principle. Reverting to a previous state means reverting a commit.

This principle changes who is responsible for applying changes.

Instead of an external CI/CD pipeline pushing updates into Kubernetes, an agent inside the cluster pulls the desired state from Git… It then applies the changes.

The security implications of this shift are significant, and they get their own section shortly.

4. Continuously Reconciled

The previous three principles describe how state gets defined and delivered.

This one describes what happens after:

Continuous reconciliation means repeatedly comparing the live cluster state with the desired state in Git. These comparisons detect changes introduced by a manual edit, an autoscaler, or a partial update. The configured sync policy determines whether ArgoCD reports the difference or corrects it automatically.

To understand why GitOps works differently, we first need to compare it with the deployment model most people already use…

CD Without GitOps vs CD With GitOps

With the four principles in place, the difference between traditional CD & GitOps is easier to see.

It is not just a philosophical shift. The two models produce different security properties and failure modes.

They also provide different levels of visibility into what runs in production…

How CD Worked Before GitOps

In a traditional push-based setup, the CI/CD pipeline carries a release from source code to the Kubernetes cluster.

It runs tests, builds a container image, and pushes the image to a registry. The deployment stage then updates Kubernetes using a command such as or .

For example, releasing version 1.5 means the pipeline updates the Deployment to use the new image. Kubernetes then replaces the existing pods according to the configured rollout strategy.

The pipeline directly initiates the deployment. The deployment stage delivers the new configuration to the cluster.

With ArgoCD, the pipeline still tests the application, builds the image, and publishes it to a registry. It then updates the image reference in the configuration repository.

For the same version 1.5 release, the pipeline changes the image tag in a Kubernetes manifest, Helm values file, or Kustomize configuration. This change becomes a Git commit rather than a deployment command executed against the cluster.

ArgoCD detects the updated configuration and compares it with the live resources. With automated sync enabled, it applies the update. With manual sync, it waits for an operator to trigger synchronization. Kubernetes then performs the rollout.

i.e., Git becomes the handoff between the two systems.

CI produces the image and records the intended version. ArgoCD handles applying the configuration to Kubernetes.

This separation also changes where deployment credentials are needed, which brings us to the security boundary between push and pull.

Push vs Pull: Security Boundary

The shift from push to pull is not just an architectural preference.

It changes where credentials live, how far a compromised system can reach, and the damage a supply chain attack can cause.

Now let’s compare the two approaches:

Push-Based: Pipeline Holds the Keys

In a push-based model, the CI pipeline needs direct access to the cluster to deploy anything.

i.e., cluster credentials live inside the CI system.

Anyone with sufficient access to the CI system or pipeline configuration could also gain access to those credentials. Every third-party action, plugin, or integration running inside the pipeline runs adjacent to them. And because pipelines are triggered by code changes, a compromised dependency runs in the pipeline. It runs in the same environment as your cluster credentials.

A compromised pipeline in this model is effectively a compromised cluster.

The attacker does not need to find a vulnerability in Kubernetes… They just need to get malicious code into the build process & let the pipeline do the rest.

The blast radius is as wide as the credentials allow.

For most engineers, those credentials have broad permissions. Restricting them precisely is operationally painful. A compromised push-based pipeline often means cluster-admin access is in the wrong hands.

Pull-Based: Cluster Holds the Keys

In a pull-based model, the cluster reaches out to Git.

The CI system never touches the cluster.

ArgoCD runs inside the cluster with scoped RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) permissions. It pulls the desired state from Git and applies it. The CI pipeline updates the Git repository when a build succeeds, and its job ends there. No cluster credentials ever leave the cluster environment.

A compromised CI system in this model could modify Git.

But modifying Git only changes the desired state. It does not directly execute anything in the cluster. ArgoCD still has to pull the change and reconcile it with the cluster. Because every change goes through Git first, you get a reviewable, auditable record before it reaches production.

And the blast radius shrinks dramatically. A compromised pipeline becomes a much less dangerous event.

Let’s look at how ArgoCD is built:

ArgoCD is not an external service you call into.

It runs as Kubernetes workloads inside the cluster it manages, in the argocd namespace. This is . The agent needs direct access to the Kubernetes API to reconcile state. Running inside the cluster provides the access & keeps cluster credentials inside the cluster.

Here are 5 core components that work together to implement the GitOps reconciliation loop:

API Server is the entry point for everything human-facing in ArgoCD.

It exposes both gRPC & REST APIs consumed by the ArgoCD UI, argocd CLI, and any external tools integrating with ArgoCD. Every user request, whether it comes from the UI, CLI, or an external integration, passes through the API Server.

Also it handles all authentication & authorization.

Before any request reaches the rest of the system, the API Server verifies who is making it and whether they have permission.

The Repo Server does one thing: render Kubernetes manifests from a Git repository.

It clones the repository, reads the source, and generates the manifests ArgoCD will apply to the cluster. It supports plain YAML, Helm charts, Kustomize overlays, and Jsonnet. Whatever format your configuration lives in, the Repo Server handles the rendering.

It’s deliberately isolated from the Application Controller.

Rendering manifests requires running Helm, Kustomize & Jsonnet. Those processes are often CPU-intensive and occasionally unstable. Keeping the Repo Server separate isolates render failures from the controller’s reconciliation loop.

3. Application Controller

The Application Controller is the heart of ArgoCD…It runs the reconciliation loop.

On every cycle, it gets the desired manifests from the Repo Server and the live cluster state from the Kubernetes API. Then it computes the diff between the two. Based on the application’s sync policy, it either alerts you to the difference or corrects it automatically.

The Application Controller runs as a StatefulSet.

(Scaling and sharding are covered later.)

Redis serves as a cache layer between Application Controller and Kubernetes API.

Without it, every UI load and every reconciliation cycle would need to query the Kubernetes API directly. At scale, this would generate unnecessary load on the Kubernetes API. Redis stores application state and cluster data so repeated reads hit the cache instead of the API.

It is worth being clear about what Redis is and is not in this context.

It is a cache, not a primary data store. ArgoCD does not depend on Redis for correctness. If Redis goes down, ArgoCD degrades gracefully. Performance suffers, but reconciliation continues.

5. Notifications Controller

Notifications Controller watches ArgoCD events & route alerts to external systems.

When an application goes OutOfSync, a sync fails, or a health check degrades, the Notifications Controller sends an alert. It uses the destination you configured, such as Slack, email, PagerDuty, or a webhook. You define triggers and templates, and the controller handles the delivery.

In most production deployments, it gets installed alongside the rest of ArgoCD. It connects ArgoCD’s internal events with the people and systems responsible for responding to them.

Together, these components form ArgoCD's control plane...

Each component has a specific responsibility:

  • API Server handles user requests.

  • Repo Server renders manifests.

  • Application Controller reconciles applications.

  • Redis caches data to reduce repeated API calls.

  • Notifications Controller reports important events.

Together, these components keep the cluster aligned with the desired state in Git.

With the architecture covered, let’s see how these components work together during reconciliation…

When you upgrade, you’ll get:

  • High-level architecture of real-world systems.

  • Deep dive into how popular real-world systems work.

  • How real-world systems handle scale, reliability & performance.

(If this newsletter has helped you become a better software engineer, consider subscribing to support my work.)

How ArgoCD Keeps Your Cluster in Sync

items.title: 11 Networking Concepts Explained in 11 Minutes
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
Computer networking is an important part of ALL systems you’ll work on in your engineering career.

While junior developers may get by with writing code, senior engineers are valued for their ability to understand how systems communicate & troubleshoot network problems.

What happens when a network connection fails?

How does data travel between devices & servers?

How do we diagnose slow connections, packet loss & routing problems?

These questions form the foundation of every reliable, high-performing system.

Right now, you’re your agent’s context engine. You write the rules files, maintain the skills, and paste in the Slack thread it missed.

But hand-curated context goes stale. And when there are conflicting answers, your agent can’t tell which is right. You pay for it in higher token bills and longer reviews.

  • The 8-levels of AI maturity and where teams get stuck

  • How a context engine curates context and resolves conflicts before your agent writes a line of code

  • Live demo: token savings in the same coding task, and use cases beyond code gen

Bonus: 2 open source tools you can use today.

(Thanks to Unblocked for partnering on this newsletter.)

Here are all the key concepts that you need to understand computer networking & become a better engineer:

Ethernet is a networking technology that connects devices within a Local Area Network ().

  1. The sender wraps an IP packet inside an Ethernet frame.

  2. Frame contains source & destination Media Access Control () addresses.

  3. The network interface sends the frame over a physical link.

  4. Network switches forward frames toward their destinations using MAC addresses.

  5. The receiver checks the frame’s Frame Check Sequence () to detect transmission errors.

Typical Ethernet speeds include 1 Gbps for desktops, 10 or 25 Gbps for servers, and 100+ Gbps for data center networks.

Imagine delivering packages between offices in the same building.

Each package carries the sender’s & recipient’s room numbers. A mailroom reads the destination and forwards the package to the correct office.

A media access control () address identifies a network card. They help devices communicate within a “local” network.

Every card ships with a 48-bit address, written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits. The first half identifies the manufacturer, while the second half identifies the card.

IP addresses move packets between networks, and MAC addresses move frames within one network. A device learns its neighbor’s MAC address by broadcasting a question through the address resolution protocol (), and then caches that answer.

Think of an IP address as a building’s street address and a MAC address as an apartment number.

A switch forwards frames between devices on the “same” network, using their MAC addresses.

A switch learns devices that are reachable through each port by reading the source MAC address of incoming frames. Then it stores these MAC address-to-port mappings in a

  • The switch forwards the frame through the port associated with the destination MAC address.

  • The switch floods the frame through all other ports in the same VLAN until it learns where the destination is located.

A switch forwards Ethernet frames within a local network using MAC addresses, while a router forwards IP packets between networks using IP addresses.

Imagine a mailroom in an office building:

The mailroom learns which office belongs to each employee & delivers letters directly to the correct room. If it doesn’t know the destination, it sends copies to every office until it learns where the recipient is.

Wi-Fi is a wireless networking technology that uses radio waves to transmit data between devices.

  • Devices send & receive data using radio signals.

  • Devices use mechanisms such as Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance () to reduce transmission collisions.

  • Wi-Fi operates on 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz bands.

  • Devices adjust transmission rates based on signal quality & interference.

  • Lost/corrupted frames require retransmission; thus reducing throughput.

The 2.4 GHz band typically provides longer range but has less available capacity & more interference.

The 5 GHz & 6 GHz bands offer wider channels and potentially higher speeds, but their signals have shorter range & weaker penetration through obstacles.

Also devices with poor signal quality transmit at lower data rates and consume more airtime. This reduces the capacity available to other devices sharing the channel.

Imagine a room where people take turns speaking.

Everyone listens before talking to avoid interruptions. If someone far away speaks slowly, others have to wait longer to finish.

A static IP address is a “fixed” IP address assigned to a device or network interface.

You configure it manually or reserve an address through Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol ().

A static IP typically remains the same across device reboots as long as its assignment remains valid. Servers, printers, routers & other devices that need predictable network addresses use static IPs.

DNS records, firewall rules & network configurations reference these stable addresses.

Think of it as a reserved parking space with your name on the sign.

The space stays assigned to you, whether you manage the reservation yourself or someone else manages it.

Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol () automatically assigns IP addresses & other network settings to devices when they join a network.

  1. The device broadcasts a message to find available DHCP servers.

  2. A DHCP server offers an IP address & network configuration.

  3. The device requests the offered address.

  4. Server confirms the assignment & grants an IP address .

(This process is called DORA.)

Plus, DHCP server provides a subnet mask, default gateway, and Domain Name System () servers.

Yet each IP address lease has a lifetime.

Devices typically renew leases before they expire. If a lease expires without renewal, the server reassigns the address to another device.

Imagine checking into a hotel:

The receptionist assigns you a room number for your stay. When you check out, the room becomes available for another guest.

A default gateway is a router that forwards traffic to destinations outside a device’s local network when “no” specific route exists.

  • The device sends traffic directly to another device on the same subnet.

  • The device forwards traffic to its default gateway.

  • Gateway uses its routing table to forward the packet toward its destination.

A laptop with IP address might use as its default gateway.

The gateway typically has an IP address on the same subnet,,, thus allowing the laptop to reach it directly.

An incorrect default gateway prevents a device from reaching “external” networks, even if local communication works.

Think of a building with one main exit.

You move between rooms inside the building without leaving. To reach another building, you must use the main exit.

A static route is a (manually) configured entry in a routing table that tells a router where to forward packets.

You specify a destination IP range & an outgoing network interface.

  • Define a destination network, such as .

  • Point the route to another router, such as .

  • The router uses the route to forward matching traffic toward its destination.

Yet static routes do not automatically learn new network paths.

If a network path fails, the static route still remains configured. Some implementations detect failures & deactivate/replace the route.

Static routes work well for cloud networking configurations.

Imagine a road sign directing drivers toward a specific town.

The sign stays in place even when the road closes, unless someone updates it or a traffic management system redirects drivers.

Open Shortest Path First () is a dynamic routing protocol that lets routers automatically discover & update routes within an Autonomous System ().

  1. Routers exchange Hello packets to discover & maintain neighboring routers.

  2. Routers flood Link-State Advertisements (s) to share network information within an OSPF area.

  3. Routers in the same area maintain a synchronized link-state database.

  4. Each router uses Dijkstra’s Shortest Path First algorithm to calculate the lowest-cost paths.

  5. When a link fails, routers propagate updated information and recalculate affected routes.

OSPF selects paths based on configurable interface costs.

Bandwidth influences these costs, but administrators could adjust them manually.

Plus, OSPF reroutes traffic after network failures. Convergence time depends on failure detection, topology size & router configuration.

Imagine every driver in a city using a shared road map.

When a road closes, the map updates, and each driver calculates a new route based on the available roads.

Internet Control Message Protocol () carries network error messages & diagnostic information. It helps devices identify problems such as unreachable destinations, expired packet lifetimes, and packets too large for a network link.

  • A router or destination host sends an ICMP message when it cannot deliver a packet.

  • A router sends an ICMP message when a packet’s Time to Live () or Hop Limit reaches zero.

  • ICMP reports when a packet exceeds the supported Maximum Transmission Unit ().

  • Tools such as use ICMP to test whether a destination responds.

Yet ICMP messages are NOT guaranteed to arrive…

Firewalls, rate limiting & network conditions could block/drop them.

ICMP helps diagnose network problems but does not directly retransmit lost application data or repair failed connections.

Imagine sending a letter that cannot reach its destination…

The post office returns a notice explaining why delivery failed, such as an invalid address or an unavailable route.

The notice helps you identify the problem, but it does not deliver the original letter.

Ping is a network diagnostic tool that tests whether a destination host responds & measures round-trip time (). It uses ICMP Echo Request & Echo Reply messages.

  1. Ping sends an ICMP Echo Request to the destination.

  2. If the destination responds, it sends an ICMP Echo Reply.

  3. Ping calculates time between sending request & receiving reply.

  4. Ping reports round-trip times & percentage of requests without replies.

Repeated tests help identify latency spikes, intermittent connectivity & potential packet loss.

Imagine knocking on a door & timing how long someone takes to answer.

A quick response suggests someone is available. A delayed response takes longer, while silence only means nobody answered.

Now you understand the basic networking concepts that help devices communicate, it’s time to explore how they work in real systems.

Look at the apps & networks you use every day and think about what happens behind the scenes.

What happens when a network link fails?

How does your laptop connect to the internet?

How do routers find the right path for packets?

How do engineers diagnose slow or failed connections?

After understanding these concepts, start applying them in your own work.

Use tools like , , and to explore network behavior. Experiment with routing configurations and troubleshoot connectivity problems.

Remember, every experienced engineer started with the fundamentals. The more you practice, the easier it becomes to understand and troubleshoot complex networks.
